summary: Describes the standardization collaboration between 3GPP2, a mobile phone standards group, and the IETF, and how they coordinate work.

plainLanguage.summary: Two clubs agree on how to share the work so their pieces fit together.

questions: how does the ietf work with 3gpp2
what is the 3gpp2 liaison in the iesg
subtitle: How the mobile standards group 3GPP2 and the IETF agreed to share drafts, contacts and meetings.

tldr.problem: 3GPP2 writes specifications for CDMA-based mobile networks, and wants them to work well with the existing Internet. The IETF owns the Internet protocols that matter to it.
tldr.mechanism: The two organizations set principles for the collaboration: each keeps its own rules, drafts are shared, named contact people are appointed on both sides, and each may take part in the other's meetings.
tldr.outcome: The document is Informational and sets no Internet standard. It gives engineers on both sides a clear route to raise concerns with the right working group.

today: RFC 3131 is an Informational RFC published in June 2001, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It borrowed guidance and text from the parallel RFC 3113, which covers the equivalent collaboration with 3GPP.

sections.title: Purpose and Ground Rules
sections.content:
RFC 3131 sets out principles and guidelines for collaboration between 3GPP2 (Third Generation Partnership Project 2) and the IETF. The stated aim is timely development of technical specifications that interoperate as much as possible with existing fixed and mobile Internet systems, devices and protocols.

The collaboration does not merge the two bodies. Each organization operates under its own rules and procedures, including those for intellectual property rights, writing specifications, approval and maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clubs want their games to fit together. Each club keeps its own rules, but they agree to work as a team.

sections.title: Why the Two Groups Collaborate
sections.content:
From the 3GPP2 side, the benefit of adopting Internet specifications has been identified. Its preferred approach is to use Internet standards unchanged when feasible, and it has no intention of duplicating work done in the IETF. If changes are needed, 3GPP2 will take its concerns directly to the appropriate IETF working group, or to an Area Director if no working group fits.

From the IETF side, the benefit is access to wireless expertise. 3GPP2 technical work is split among Technical Specification Groups (TSGs):

  • TSG-A and TSG-C: radio access networks based on CDMA, and so the physical transport.
  • TSG-N: mobility management and other core network protocols and functions.
  • TSG-P: data services and applications.
  • TSG-S: service and system aspects, including overall architecture, security and operation and maintenance.
sections.plainLanguage: One club knows a lot about radio and phones, and the other knows a lot about the Internet. Working together lets each use what the other is good at.

sections.title: Sharing Documents and Communicating
sections.content:
Both organizations encourage sharing drafts of mutual interest. 3GPP2 working documents are public and grouped by meeting. Its specifications are published once they have completed a 15-day Steering Committee review. IETF documents, including preliminary Internet Drafts, are available on its web site and on mirror sites.

Informal communication at working level is encouraged whenever possible. Most IETF technical discussion and decision making happens on mailing lists, and interested people are advised to subscribe. 3GPP2 mailing lists are not open to the general public, so the RFC recommends discussing work of mutual interest on the relevant IETF lists.

When needed, formal communication is also allowed. IETF Area Directors and 3GPP2 technical leadership are encouraged and authorized to facilitate it.
sections.plainLanguage: The clubs agree to leave their notes where the other can read them. Because one club's chat room is private, they will talk in the other club's open chat room.

sections.title: Rapporteurs and the 3GPP2 Liaison
sections.content:
3GPP2 sets up an IETF rapporteur function in its Steering Committee. The appointed people are the first contact point in 3GPP2 for the collaboration, and work with the concerned working groups and TSGs.

On the IETF side, the preferred way for any organization to work with the IETF is through its working groups. Still, the RFC proposes appointing a specific person in the IESG as a 3GPP2 liaison. That person is the first contact for administrative matters that cannot easily be handled another way. The role does not expect attendance at 3GPP2 meetings or taking part in its administrative processes, and the work is expected to be done by electronic mail. The liaison cannot make exceptions to IETF policies and procedures.
sections.plainLanguage: Each club names one person to be the go-to helper for the other club. The helper can point people the right way, but cannot change the other club's rules.

sections.title: Participation in Meetings
sections.content:
To help information flow, the IETF can appoint an observer, case by case, to represent it at 3GPP2 technical meetings. IETF meetings are open to any interested individuals, and 3GPP2 partners or individual members can take part under the existing IETF procedures.

3GPP2 meetings are also open to any interested individual, but such individuals do not have voting privileges. The RFC has no real security content: it says this kind of non-protocol document does not directly affect the security of the Internet.
sections.plainLanguage: Visitors are welcome at both clubs' meetings. At the 3GPP2 club, guests can listen and talk but cannot vote.
